title: FetchX API changelog
description: Changes to the FetchX API at /v1, newest first. Each release has a version (docs/openapi.json info.version is the latest) and a date. Breaking changes, to a route or to a field of an answer, are announced here as deprecations first: each names the route or field, the version and date it was deprecated, what replaces it, and its sunset date, at least 30 days later. Until the sunset the API still serves it, and a deprecated route marks its responses with Deprecation and Sunset headers; afterwards a retired route answers 410 Gone with error.details.replacement.

policy.compatibility: Every field the API reference documents in an answer is covered, as well as every route. FetchX does not remove or rename a field, change its type, let it be null or missing where it always had a value, stop sending a value it lists, or change what a value means, without a deprecation here at least 30 days before the change. Until then the old field or value is still sent. Additions ship without notice and are listed here when they ship: new fields, new values in a list of values, new error codes, new routes and new optional request fields. A client should ignore fields it does not know and treat a value it does not know as other. Follow /changelog.xml (Atom) or /changelog.json to hear about a deprecation the day it is announced.

releases.title: Browser sessions you drive with Playwright

changes.text: POST /v1/browser-sessions starts a browser (Camoufox, a hardened Firefox) that you drive yourself with Playwright: connect to its ws_url with playwright.firefox.connect and your API key in the Authorization header, and drive browser.contexts[0]. allow_hosts is required: every request a page or a frame makes, cross-origin frames included, reaches FetchX first and one to a host off the list is refused before it leaves FetchX; workers' requests and WebSockets are held to the list by FetchX's proxy, and refused ones are listed in blocked_requests (WebSockets as websocket, with their wss:// origin, and counted in websockets.refused). Your own context.route handlers see every request FetchX lets through. Saved logins and secrets are typed with POST /v1/browser-sessions/{id}/fill and never reach your client. A session runs up to ttl_s (30 to 900 s, default 300) and closes when your client is idle or gone for idle_ttl_s (10 to 120 s, default 60); DELETE closes it and GET reads its receipt, kept for 90 days. Feature id browser_sessions.

Browser sessions are billed once per session, when it ends: a flat price (GET /v1/prices browser_sessions), plus residential traffic past the included MB, capped at max_credits. A session whose browser failed (close_reason error) costs nothing. Open sessions are limited per project (GET /v1/me concurrency.browser_sessions), and each also counts as a running request.

Browser sessions run Playwright 1.62.1 (playwright.version on each session); connect with a 1.62.x client, as another version is refused with HTTP 428 at connect. A move to a newer Playwright is announced here at least 14 days before sessions change.

releases.title: Request ids, usage per key, the compatibility promise

changes.text: Every answer carries an X-Request-Id header, and every JSON answer from /v1, success or error, carries the same id as request_id (req_ and 24 hex digits). It names the HTTP call: a fetch keeps its own id. Log it, and quote it when you ask about a call; FetchX can find the call, and the fetch it started, from it. Feature id request_ids.

GET /v1/usage takes key_id: used, by_step and daily then count only requests made with that API key, and the keys it was rotated from or to. The answer says which (key_id, key_ids); balance stays the project's. An id that is not one of the project's keys is 400 invalid_request with error.details.field key_id. Feature id usage_by_key.

The changelog's policy now states the compatibility promise for answer fields as well as routes: no field is removed, renamed, retyped, made nullable or optional, and no listed value dropped or redefined, without a deprecation here at least 30 days ahead. Deprecations can now name a field (field) as well as a route (path).
POST /v1/estimate counts the project's own limit of requests at once, when FetchX has raised it for that project, instead of the default.

releases.title: Forms in frames, blocked requests to reserved names, empty JSON bodies

changes.text: A form that a caller's action submits inside a frame (such as a sign-in form framed from another host on allow_hosts) is sent, as one in the top frame always was. It was refused, and the frame showed the browser's blocked-page error.

With allow_hosts, a request the page makes to a host off the list is listed in data.blocked_requests also when the host is a reserved or private name (such as outside.example) that FetchX would refuse anyway.
A DELETE or GET sent with Content-Type: application/json and no body is no longer refused with 400 invalid_request.
fixtures.fetchx.ai pages no longer carry Cloudflare's analytics script, so they load no third-party scripts.

releases.title: FetchX's public test site

changes.text: https://fixtures.fetchx.ai is FetchX's public test site, and POST /v1/fetch may now fetch it (and its framed form on frame.fixtures.fetchx.ai); the rest of fetchx.ai stays refused with url_not_allowed. It has a sign-in form with a CSRF token (fixture-user / fixture-password), a redirect chain that sets a cookie on each hop, an echo of what was sent, a page that fills in late inside a shadow root, a form in a cross-origin frame, CAPTCHA pages using each vendor's test keys, and a page that tries to send its cookie elsewhere, so your acceptance tests for actions, allow_hosts, redirects and capture can run through FetchX. Feature id fixtures.

releases.title: Per-request secrets and unstored requests

changes.text: POST /v1/fetch takes secrets: up to 8 named values (a password or token, 4 characters to 4096 bytes) for this request only, each with the https origins it may go to, which must be in allow_hosts. A fill_secret action types one into a field whose frame is at one of its origins (else action_failed with secret_origin_mismatch). Over HTTP, {{secret.<name>}} in body or a header value is filled in when it is sent, form-encoded or JSON-escaped to match the body's content type; the URL's origin must be one of the secret's, and a GET or HEAD with placeholders needs render: never. FetchX never stores, logs or returns a secret's value: wherever a page shows or echoes it (as typed, URL-encoded, form-encoded, JSON-escaped or base64) it comes back as [REDACTED:<name>]. Feature id secrets.

While a secret is loaded, anything the page sends that carries it to an origin the secret does not name (a script's request, a form, a redirect over HTTP) is stopped, and the request fails with secret_egress_blocked (next.action check_origins), free. Once a secret has been typed or sent, FetchX makes no further attempt on any route, so a sign-in is never sent twice. secrets_used on the result (top level, beside status) and in GET /v1/fetch lists names the secrets that were used, never their values; an attempt that used one has secrets_used: true.

POST /v1/fetch takes store: false (always false with secrets): the first read of the finished result with its body (the 200 answer, or a poll of GET /v1/fetch/{id}) returns the content in full, with the body always inline, and deletes it; unread content is deleted at the latest 15 minutes after the request finished. After that the result keeps only its summary (status, page_status, credits, error, attempts, secrets_used) with data null, and its content, screenshot and network routes and POST /v1/fetch/{id}/next answer 410 not_stored. The kept request has no headers, body or action values.

secrets is refused with 400 secret_not_allowed_here (error.details.field names the clash) together with screenshot, extract, capture.unmask or webhook_url, and in batches. POST /v1/feedback refuses a request made with secrets.

releases.title: Browser actions, host allowlists, manual redirects, concurrency and USD prices

changes.text: POST /v1/fetch takes actions: up to 50 steps for a browser to take, in order, once the page has loaded (wait, wait_for_url, click, hover, fill, type, press, select, scroll, navigate, evaluate, wait_for_response). They run in one tab and one page, and data.actions has one result per action, with what each evaluate returned. data.body is the page as the last action left it. Billed as one browser step with nothing per action; a request whose action failed fails with action_failed (error.details.action_index) and is free. With actions, timeout_ms may be up to 300000. Feature id actions.

The wait_for_response action waits for the first response to a request that started after the previous action and that completes, matched by URL, method and status, and returns it in data.actions[i].response: the exact URL, the real status, headers and body (up to 2 MB), as the browser's network layer saw it. With capture, every captured call has action_index (the action that set it off) and complete, and phase actions. Feature id capture_actions.

POST /v1/fetch takes allow_hosts: the only hosts a request may reach (exact names or *.suffix). In a browser every request and connection to a host off the list is refused and listed in data.blocked_requests; over HTTP a redirect off the list is not followed. allow_passive_subresources lets scripts, styles, fonts and images load from other hosts without cookies (data.passive_offlist_hosts). Feature id allow_hosts.

POST /v1/fetch takes redirect: manual, to get a redirect itself instead of where it leads (a login that answers 302 with its cookies): data.status_code is the 3xx, data.final_url the request URL and data.location where it points. Manual redirects are HTTP only. Feature id redirect_manual.

Over HTTP, data.redirects lists the redirects followed (URL, status, where each pointed, the names of the cookies it set), and data.cookies has the cookies every hop set, each with the hop that set it, not only those for the final URL.
POST /v1/fetch takes all_headers: true, which returns the response's headers as sent in data.raw_headers: in order, with each Set-Cookie, and over HTTP the site's own casing.

GET /v1/me has concurrency: the project's requests-at-once limit (requests.limit, 10 unless raised) and how many are running now (requests.running). It counts every kind of request, HTTP or browser, next pages and batch items included.

GET /v1/me has features: what this FetchX supports, by feature id (actions, allow_hosts, batches, capture, capture_actions, estimate, extract, feedback, key_limits, limits, logins, next_page, redirect_manual, usd). Check for an id before relying on a newer feature; new ids are listed here as they ship.
429 too_many_requests on POST /v1/fetch and POST /v1/fetch/{id}/next names the limit it hit: error.details.limit is requests, with max (the limit) and running, next to retry_after_seconds.
GET /v1/balance has usd_per_credit and currency (USD): what one credit costs in USD, from the pack the project bought last, or the smallest pack when it has bought none.
GET /v1/prices has packs: each credit pack on sale with its credits, its price in USD and INR, and its USD price per credit.

releases.title: Saved site logins

changes.text: POST /v1/logins saves a site's username and password, encrypted. When a page a request reads asks for a sign-in on that site (its host or a subdomain, over https), FetchX fills in the sign-in form in a browser, solves a captcha in the form if one shows, sends it, and keeps the signed-in session for the project's later requests. The password is never returned or logged, never typed on another host, and taken out of stored pages and network captures. GET, PATCH and DELETE /v1/logins/{id} read, change and delete a login; GET /v1/logins lists them. Free; up to 50 per project.

POST /v1/fetch takes login: a saved login's id to sign in with (for a sign-in on another domain, such as an SSO provider), or false to never sign in. Left out, the project's only login for the request's registrable domain is used. A request that sends its own Cookie or Authorization header uses no saved login.

A failed request says login_required when the site asked for a sign-in and FetchX had no saved login for it (next.action provide_credentials), and login_failed when the site did not accept the saved login (next.action update_login, or retry_later when the sign-in got no clear answer). page_status is login_required for both, and neither is charged. Each browser attempt that signed in reports sign_in. Once FetchX has sent a login on a page the request makes no further attempts, and a login the site rejected or that needs a one-time code is not typed again until you update it.

releases.title: MTCaptcha solving

changes.text: Browser steps solve MTCaptcha when it stands in the way: shown and not verified, and either the only thing left to fill in its form or on a wall page with no form. It costs the same 10 credits as other captchas, only on a successful request. A widget that verifies by itself is left alone, and so is one on a form that still needs your details (a sign-in): a token alone cannot get past it, so nothing is spent.
vendor (on attempts and on blocked or rate-limited errors) can be mtcaptcha when that is the only protection a wall shows.

A URL's #fragment is kept for the browser: it is never sent to the site, but a browser opens the page with it, and next pages keep it. An app route (#/... or #!/...) makes auto start in a browser, since plain HTTP gets the same empty app for every route.

A browser page that shows nothing yet (an app still loading) is not read as finished, and a page that sends itself on while it is read (such as an app's redirect to its sign-in) is followed, so the result is the page it went to.

releases.title: Capped keys and one-step approval in Connect

changes.text: Connect: POST /api/control/connect/start takes limits (credits_per_day, credits_per_month, and expires_at or expires_in_days), the same limits a console key can have. The approval page shows them and the user may change or remove them before approving; the key gets the limits the user approved, returned as limits on start and on the connected claim, and by GET /v1/me.

Connect: start returns verification_uri_complete (RFC 8628), a link that carries the user code in its fragment. The approval page shows the code for the user to check against their tool instead of typing it, and keeps it across signing in.

Connect: a user with no project, or who wants a new one, creates it on the approval page and approves in one step (decision with project_name instead of project_id). A new account's first project gets the trial credits, as in the console.
Connect requests last 20 minutes (expires_in 1200), time to sign up and approve. Clients should accept expires_in up to 3600.
The JavaScript Connect helper takes limits (CLI: --credits-per-day, --credits-per-month, --expires-in-days), prints the link that carries the code, and returns the key's limits.

The Python SDK (0.2.0) has Connect: connect(), or connect_start() and connect_finish() for agents whose tool calls must return quickly, and python -m fetchx connect. It keeps the key in an owner-only ~/.config/fetchx/credentials file (XDG_CONFIG_HOME and %APPDATA% respected), which FetchX() reads when FETCHX_TOKEN is not set. It is on PyPI: pip install fetchx-sdk.

releases.title: Prices without a key

changes.text: GET /v1/prices needs no API key: the credits each step costs (with the route classes it covers and the traffic it includes), what a solved captcha, residential traffic past the included MB and extraction add, and the trial credits a new account gets. Any origin may call it, so a tool can quote a site's cost before the user signs up.
The JavaScript and Python clients and the Python SDK have prices(). The SDK's FakeFetchX answers GET /v1/prices with the default table.

releases.title: The shape of a JSON body

changes.text: formats: ["skeleton"] returns data.skeleton instead of the whole body: the root type, every field once as a JSONPath ($.items[*].price) with its type (string|null when it varies), how often it was seen and, for arrays, how many elements, and a sample (the body with every array cut to its first element and long strings cut short). A few KB however large the body, so a client or a language model can see the shape of a JSON API before reading megabytes; truncated says when fields were left out. Null when the body is not JSON. Free, like the other formats.

releases.title: Feedback on how FetchX handled a page

changes.text: POST /v1/feedback reports a page FetchX could not get or got wrong: name the request (fetch_id) or the URL and method, say what you saw (kind: blocked_via_fetchx_ok_from_home, wrong_content, extract_wrong or other), and add a message and evidence from where it worked (status_code, final_url, content_type, body_excerpt, client). FetchX keeps a copy of what it did with the request, so the report stays useful after the result expires. Free; up to 100 reports a day per project; kept 90 days.
GET /v1/feedback/{id} shows where a report stands (received, reviewing, resolved or dismissed) and FetchX staff's reply.

releases.title: Credit limits and expiry for API keys

changes.text: An API key can have its own credit limit per day and per month (UTC) and an expiry, set in the console when the key is made or later. Hand a capped key to a tool, a scheduler or a teammate without handing over the whole balance. Rotating a key keeps its limits and what it has spent.

A request that would take a key past its limit is refused before anything is sent: 402 key_limit_reached, with error.details.limit (credits_per_day or credits_per_month), credits, used, remaining, needed and resets_at. A request reserves no more than the limit has left. A batch whose key reaches its limit pauses with paused_reason key_limit_reached and starts again by itself when the limit resets.
An expired key answers 401 api_key_expired with error.details.expired_at, instead of unauthorized.
GET /v1/me has limits: credits_per_day and credits_per_month (each limit, used, remaining and resets_at, or null) and expires_at.

releases.title: Network capture on browser pages, GET /v1/me, and Retry-After when FetchX is busy

changes.text: capture on POST /v1/fetch (and /next, and batch items): a page read in a browser records its own network calls, so you can find the JSON or GraphQL call that carries the data and fetch it directly with render: never. capture: true records documents, XHR and fetch calls; an object sets types (also script, eventsource, other), max_requests (up to 1000, default 200), max_body_bytes (up to 10 MB, default 2 MB), bodies (text, none or all), first_party_only, include_trackers and unmask. Capture is free. With render: auto it makes FetchX use a browser, which POST /v1/estimate shows.

The result has a top-level network field: calls captured, calls dropped by reason (trackers, excluded_types, third_party, over_limit), truncated, the attempt whose browser recorded them, complete, expires_at, list_url and har_url. A failed request still has its capture.

GET /v1/fetch/{id}/network lists the calls in order, filtered by type, content_type, host (or *.example.com), first_party, status (200 or 2xx), page, phase and contains (values the response body holds, compared without case; a JSON body is also searched as parsed). GET /v1/fetch/{id}/network/{index} gives one call with its headers and bodies (a body over 1 MB by body_url, GET /v1/fetch/{id}/network/{index}/body). GET /v1/fetch/{id}/network.har is the capture as a HAR 1.2 file for browser developer tools. All need fetch:read.

Each call has phase: warmup (FetchX's own visit to a protected site's home page before yours), load, scroll (after scrolling started) or replay (getting back to the earlier page on /next), and frame: main or child. Cookie, Set-Cookie, Authorization and token, session, password and API-key headers are masked as <masked len=N sha=xxxxxx> unless you send unmask: true. Analytics, advertising and consent calls are left out unless include_trackers is true.

Captured calls are kept with the request's content: 7 days, or until DELETE /v1/fetch/{id}, then 410 content_expired. A request made without capture answers 404 capture_not_found. capture with render: never, a method other than GET, or a route without a browser is refused with invalid_request, error.details.field capture.
GET /v1/me: the project (project_id stays the same when a key is rotated), this key's id, name and prefix, and its scopes. Any valid key may call it.
A 503 unavailable now always carries a Retry-After header and retry_after_seconds (30 unless FetchX knows better), also when the API is up but its fetch engine does not answer.

releases.title: Blocked IPs move to another country, captchas on a site's home page are solved, and walls say whose they are

changes.text: When you leave country to FetchX and a site keeps blocking one country's IPs (two blocks in a row), the next tries use another country's IPs, such as the UK, Canada or Australia, and later requests to that site start in the country that got through. attempts[].country shows which country each attempt used. Requests that set country stay in it.

Each new browser session now looks like a different device to the site, not only a different IP: graphics card, core count, sound device and language list change with it, as on real computers. Sites whose bot protection had tied FetchX's sessions together should block less.

block_resources now applies only where no bot protection is watching. On a site whose bot protection has walled FetchX, and on any attempt after a wall, the browser loads the page's images, video and fonts too, since a bot check can notice files that never load. Such pages can use more residential traffic.

When a browser step starts at a protected site's home page and meets a captcha there, FetchX now solves it and goes on to your page, instead of giving up that IP. attempts[].warmup says solved, and attempts[].captcha lists the solve (10 credits, charged only when the request succeeds).

challenge.vendor and attempts[].challenge now name the bot protection behind a wall more often: also when the wall came as a 429, when its captcha frame sits far down a large page, and from the protection's own headers and cookies. New values: kasada, and arkose when only the captcha provider is known.

releases.title: Pages as JSON in your own shape

changes.text: extract on POST /v1/fetch: send a small JSON Schema and get the page back as JSON in data.extract. A root object is one record; a root array, with a description of one record, gets every record on a list page. data.extract_report says how sure each value is and why a missing one is null. Every value is checked against the page, so a value the page does not show comes back null, never guessed. Next pages keep the same extract.
Fields you list in the schema's required work like expect: a page that does not show them fails with content_missing and is not charged, and attempts[].missing names them as extract:<field>.

Extraction costs 10 credits per started 25,000 tokens of page text read (one unit on most pages, 60 at most), charged only when the request succeeds. credits.breakdown shows extract_tokens and extract_credits, and POST /v1/estimate counts it.

503 extract_unavailable: when FetchX cannot read pages into JSON, a request with extract is refused before anything is fetched. If extraction fails after the fetch, the request fails with extract_unavailable. Neither is charged. Wait retry_after_seconds, or send it without extract.

Batches take extract too, in defaults or per item. While extraction is unavailable, a batch whose items ask for it pauses with paused_reason extract_unavailable and tries again by itself after 5 minutes; nothing is charged meanwhile.
The json format (the body parsed as JSON). A JSON API's response is in body; use extract to get a page as JSON.

releases.title: Batches: many URLs in one job, run at each site's pace

changes.text: POST /v1/batches: up to 1000 URLs, or POST /v1/fetch bodies laid over shared defaults, in one job. Every item is checked first, and one bad item refuses the batch and names it (items[3].formats). FetchX starts the items itself at the pace each site can take, so you need no pacing loop of your own; each item is charged only if it succeeds.
GET /v1/batches, GET /v1/batches/{id}, GET /v1/batches/{id}/items (by index, or with order=finished as a feed of what finished since your last read) and POST /v1/batches/{id}/cancel.

Batch webhooks: each item's result as it finishes (fetch.finished, with batch: {id, index}), then batch.finished when it ends or batch.paused when the balance runs out. A batch that paused starts again by itself after a top-up.
Every webhook delivery carries an X-FetchX-Event header naming the event, and every result has batch: {id, index} for a batch item, or null.

The JavaScript and Python clients: submitBatch, getBatch, listBatches, batchItems, cancelBatch, and batchResults to follow results until the batch ends (submit_batch, batch_results and so on in Python).

releases.title: Cost estimates, status and clear answers for routes that are gone

changes.text: POST /v1/estimate: what a request, or a batch of up to 1000, would cost and how long it would take, before anything is sent or reserved. It uses what recent requests to each site took, the price table and your max_credits, and says when a request would be refused or is likely to fail.

GET /v1/status: the API's state, its components and any incident or maintenance notice, without an API key. The status page at https://fetchx.ai/status shows the same, with 90 days of history, and keeps working when the API does not answer.

During maintenance that pauses the API, every /v1 route except GET /v1/status answers 503 with error.code maintenance, a Retry-After header and error.details.status_url. Wait and retry; nothing was sent or charged.

Routes that have been retired answer 410 Gone with error.code route_retired and error.details.replacement, and unknown routes answer 404 route_not_found with links to the docs, this changelog and the status page, instead of a bare 404.
Deprecated routes carry Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers (RFC 9745, RFC 8594) until they are retired. None are deprecated today.
This changelog, also as JSON at https://fetchx.ai/changelog.json and as an Atom feed at https://fetchx.ai/changelog.xml.
While FetchX restarts, the API answers 503 with error.code unavailable and a Retry-After header instead of an HTML error page. Resend with the same idempotency_key.
The JavaScript and Python clients wait out 503 maintenance like any other 503, up to retries times.

releases.title: Page status, content checks and cost on every answer

changes.text: page_status (content, not_found, empty, challenge or error) and challenge (vendor, walls, whether it was passed and how) on every result.
expect: a selector, text or minimum markdown length the page must show. A page without it fails with content_missing and is not charged.
block_resources (default true): a browser does not download images, video, audio or web fonts, which cuts residential traffic.
credits.breakdown (step, captcha and traffic credits) and credits.balance on every result; credits.charged is 0 on failures. GET /v1/balance returns the credits available now.
error.next.retry_with_new_key on every failure says whether the same request can get a different answer with a new idempotency_key.
body is a format, and the default. A request whose formats leave it out does not get the raw body back.
include_body on POST /v1/fetch. Use formats instead; GET /v1/fetch/{id}?include_body=false still works.

releases.title: Scrolling and next pages

changes.text: scroll: auto (up to 10 screens, the default), off, or 1 to 50 screens.

POST /v1/fetch/{id}/next gets the page after a result's page on the same session: a next link, a next button or more scrolling. data.next_page says whether there is one, and data.page which page this is.
A page read deeper than 10 screens reserves more credits, for the traffic it may load.

releases.title: Browser steps explain themselves

changes.text: attempts[] report a browser step's warm-up visit (warmup), whether a bot check cleared by itself (wall), whether the page finished filling in (content, content_ms, screens, scroll) and its requests let through or refused.
A rendered page that answered but shows next to nothing is not a success and is not charged; FetchX tries a fresh IP.
After a wall on a residential browser, FetchX draws a fresh IP from the other provider at once instead of resting the route.
timeout_ms defaults to 120 s, which leaves room for a captcha solve.

releases.title: One API

changes.text: POST /v1/fetch gets any public URL in auto mode: the cheapest route first, then datacenter and residential IPs and a real browser, solving captchas on the way, starting at the route known to work for the site.
GET /v1/fetch, GET and DELETE /v1/fetch/{id}, GET /v1/fetch/{id}/content and /screenshot, and GET /v1/usage.
One credit balance. A request is charged only when it succeeds, at the price of the step that got the data.

The /v2 API (fetch, render, scrape, operations, sessions, capabilities, access profiles, recipes, artifacts and usage) and the earlier /v1 workflow, job, operation, profile and render routes. Since 1.4.0 they answer 410 Gone.

retired.note: The /v2 API was replaced by one API at /v1.
